item.title: Tracking and Limiting Unsupported Claim Propagation in Multi-Agent LLM Systems: A Provenance-Aware Framework
item.description: arXiv:2611.26957v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This research examines how unsupported claims change as they move through multi-agent pipelines. It also examines whether preserving provenance can reduce these changes. We test both homogeneous and heterogeneous pipelines. Homogeneous pipelines use the same model across agents, while heterogeneous pipelines use different models. We compare the baseline with a provenance-aware framework. The framework passes each claim with its support status, source, evidence and transmission history. No new evidence is introduced during transmission. We measure changes in claim meaning, unsupported detail accretion, semantic drift, and provenance preservation. These metrics show whether the framework limits unsupported changes as claims pass between agents.
item.dc:creator: Zijia Cao, Hanqing Dou

item.title: Testing for Coordination Failures in Cooperative Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
item.description: arXiv:2611.27368v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Deep parallel cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning (CMARL)} trains multiple agents that all act at every time step to optimize a common objective. Like single-agent RL, CMARL can produce unsafe behaviors that violate implicit safety requirements not captured by the reward, and these behaviors are hard to explain. However, testing CMARL policies for safety has received less attention than the safety testing of single-agent RL policies. In this paper, we propose DisQ, a test case selection method that identifies failure-revealing states in value-based CMARL by exploiting a signal specific to trained Q-learning agents. The signal is the Q-value gap, an explainable metric that flags a state when the agents' estimates of the achievable return diverge by more than a calibrated threshold. DisQ selects such states for execution and skips those without a gap. Our experiments in four CMARL benchmark environments show that, in most of the evaluated configurations, DisQ improves failure detection over single-agent RL testing methods applied to CMARL, namely random testing and search-based testing with genetic algorithms. Our main contributions are the Q-value gap, an indicator of potential miscoordination computable from a single state without executing the system, and DisQ, a test case selection method that adapts existing single-agent testing methods to CMARL.
item.dc:creator: Dennis Gross, J{\o}rn Eirik Betten, Helge Spieker

item.title: Communication-constrained multiagent risk estimation: a simulation benchmark for adult sore throat
item.description: arXiv:2611.27468v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Distributed predictive agents may need to approach a shared estimate under limited, unreliable communication. We evaluated classical symmetric pairwise gossip among five agents initialized from frozen calibrated predictions in a synthetic adult sore-throat benchmark. Ninety runs across three fixed generator families supplied 270,000 underlying test encounters, each observed through four missingness views. Complete, ring and star graphs were compared at eight interaction budgets and transaction failure probabilities of 0, 0.2 and 0.5. The coordination extension was designed after inspection of the predictive benchmark and is exploratory. Outcomes were disagreement around the conserved arithmetic mean and its exact decomposition of mean-agent Brier error. In the base view at eight attempted pairs and 0.2 failure, disagreement variance was 0.000109 for the complete graph, 0.000134 for the ring and 0.000175 for the star. The paired complete-minus-ring difference was -0.000024 (95% Monte Carlo interval -0.000030 to -0.000019). The centralized mean had base Brier 0.069781, compared with 0.069368 for Kumo alone. Agreement therefore does not establish superiority to the strongest individual predictor. Code, fixed probability inputs and results support replay without model refitting. The study quantifies finite-budget coordination under specified simulation assumptions; it proposes no new gossip algorithm and establishes no clinical accuracy or utility.
item.dc:creator: Anas H. Alzahrani

item.title: Epistemic Social Learning: Latent Behavioral Structure under Endogenous Multi-Agent Interaction
item.description: arXiv:2611.27545v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In multi-agent interaction, a learner's actions shape the observations from which it infers other agents' behavior. A behavioral model may predict these observations well yet support poor adaptation when opponents change. We introduce Epistemic Social Learning (ESL), which couples fast, interaction-specific Bayesian beliefs with slower online learning of population-shared behavioral prototypes. Belief-conditioned decisions influence subsequent observations and, in turn, the representations learned from them. Under explicit regularity and averaging assumptions, we provide a conditional stochastic-approximation characterization of these coupled dynamics. Across twelve synthetic $3\times3$ cooperative, coordination, and adversarial games, ESL achieves the lowest aggregate post-switch regret among the evaluated online latent-adaptation methods, including a switch-aware Bayesian filter. Additional experiments examine observation loss, noise, and asymmetric incentives. These findings illustrate how predictive fit can differ from decision-relevant adaptation under policy-dependent interaction.
item.dc:creator: Jainendra Shukla, Dhruv Jaiswal, Divyanshi Beniwal, Kiriti Kanjilal

item.title: Bringing AI Assistance to the Beznau Nuclear Power Plant: A Hierarchical System of LLM Agents for Reactor Monitoring
item.description: arXiv:2611.27556v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Beznau Unit 1 in Switzerland, in operation since 1969, is the most experienced nuclear reactor still running worldwide. Five decades of incremental modernization have left its monitoring systems, alarm logs, variable catalogs, technical specifications and investigation reports in separate silos that were never designed to be queried together. As a result, investigating a core instrumentation anomaly means slow, manual gathering of knowledge scattered across databases, documents, and experienced colleagues. We present a hierarchical multi-agent assistant built on large language models (LLMs) to support these investigations and reduce the need for tedious manual searches in SAP systems. An orchestrating agent breaks down an engineer's question and hands the parts to specialized sub-agents, each with read-only access to one source. Domain expertise is written as natural-language procedures that plant engineers can read, review and revise. The system is strictly advisory, with every answer traced back to its sources. We also report organizational lessons from introducing agentic AI into a culture built on safety, traceability and conservative change. Beyond the technical architecture, the Beznau case study examines how an assistant can be introduced into a setting where evidence must be traceable, changes carefully reviewed, and operational decisions retained by plant personnel, paving the way for the responsible use of agentic AI in industrial plant monitoring.
item.dc:creator: Wenqi Zhou, Leonardo Baldo, Edwin Kolbe, Manuel Arias Chao

item.title: A Cognitive Agentic AI Framework for Interactive Process Analysis and Optimization
item.description: arXiv:2611.27725v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Complex multivariable process analysis and optimization require coordinated access to simulation, structured data, machine learning (ML), optimization, and scientific literature, often across disconnected software tools. We present a Cognitive Agentic AI Framework (CAAF) that enables interactive, iterative process investigation through natural-language prompts within an established flowsheet. Following harness-engineering principles, CAAF assigns task interpretation, planning, knowledge synthesis, and context management to a large language model while delegating numerical calculations to specialized tools. Dedicated providers connect databases, scientific-document retrieval, ML-assisted Bayesian optimization (BO), and COCO process simulation. The framework is demonstrated on methyl acetate production. Guided by successive prompts, an engineer explored multivariable relationships, conducted 4,000 BO iterations to maximize carbon conversion yield (C-Yield) and minimize specific energy cost (C-SEC), refined operating bounds, and verified selected candidates through process simulation. Re-simulation of 16 candidates within the restricted domain showed close agreement with ML predictions, with a mean absolute C-Yield error of 0.0085 (0.85 percentage points). The highest BO-derived C-Yield, verified by COCO, was 0.921 versus approximately 0.81 in the initial dataset, an improvement of about 11 percentage points. CAAF also detects and reports non-converged simulations, excludes invalid outputs, and continues subsequent evaluations. The results demonstrate how human-guided agentic coordination can combine engineering tools for iterative analysis and optimization with rigorous simulation-based verification under a fixed process topology.
item.dc:creator: Trung Ngoc Trinha, Roman Tschentscher, Trong Dong Nguyen, Trung Thanh Nguyen, Anna Trubetskaya

item.title: Federated KPI Aggregation with Local Privacy Constraints and Coordinated OLAP Roll-Ups
item.description: arXiv:2611.26709v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Cross-organizational KPI analysis can require aggregated results from independently administered data warehouses without centralizing detailed records. To limit disclosure from small local groups, a site can require a minimum number of contributing records before releasing a KPI value for a group. If each site applies this rule independently, different local contributions may be suppressed and the combined KPI can become incomplete. This paper investigates whether OLAP granularity can be coordinated before local query results are released so that all sites satisfy their local minimum-cohort rules and contribute at the same analytical level. The proposed method selects the least-generalized common roll-up accepted by every site. Site agents coordinate current capabilities and approved local execution across independently administered sites, with privacy checks and aggregate computation remaining deterministic local functions. In a four-site prototype, coordinated roll-up retained all contributions and reproduced the corresponding centralized result, compared with 78.3% retained under independent suppression. A capability-change experiment showed fewer candidate checks and replies and no unsupported requests when current site-agent state was used. The results demonstrate the feasibility of federated KPI aggregation under local privacy constraints through coordinated granularity selection and agent-based coordination.
item.dc:creator: Felix H\"arer

item.title: SecretAgent: A Multi-Agent Framework for Privacy Protection against Vision Language Models
item.description: arXiv:2611.26936v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) can infer private information from shared images, including locations, personally identifiable information (PII), and personal attributes such as age and sex, even from medical images. Adversarial perturbations can protect such information against black-box VLMs, but existing methods overlook image quality and introduce visible artifacts into the images they protect. We present SecretAgent, the first general multi-agent framework that protects image privacy against VLMs while preserving visual fidelity. LLM agents iteratively locate the visual evidence that reveals private information and adapt an invisible perturbation to the target VLM's answers and to an appearance reviewer agent, which rejects any candidate with visible artifacts. We instantiate SecretAgent with two complementary variants: SecretAgent-Gradient optimizes the perturbation through six surrogate encoders for cross-model transferability, and the gradient-free SecretAgent-Tool composes procedural noise and achieves the best perceptual fidelity on three of the five datasets. Experiments on four privacy applications (geolocation, PII, facial, and medical) across five datasets and six VLMs show that SecretAgent preserves image quality substantially better than existing methods while achieving state-of-the-art privacy protection in every application, and that its protection transfers to other VLMs.
item.dc:creator: Minda Zhao, Yue Zhang, Mengyu Wang

item.title: Contexture: Runtime Context Eviction for High-Throughput Agent Serving
item.description: arXiv:2611.26980v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: LLM agents such as Hermes, OpenClaw, and Codex repeatedly resend growing execution histories, increasing shared GPU key-value (KV) cache demand in high-bandwidth memory (HBM). We show that shared KV capacity limits agent-serving throughput. Existing context-reduction methods lack global cache-state visibility, while runtime KV managers lack tool-execution information. Tracing tokens to their originating tool operations reveals that later operations supersede earlier outputs and associated turns, identifying 64% of recorded final-history tokens as removal candidates. We present Contexture, a harness- and model-agnostic architecture for runtime context eviction. Contexture separates the harness's full conversation history from the model's execution context, reducing subsequent requests' KV demand without modifying harness logic or model execution. It combines tool-execution information with global visibility into shared KV pressure and prefix residency: supersession identifies removal candidates, while runtime state determines when removal justifies sacrificing cached computation. This coordination reduces memory demand and decode KV traffic while limiting re-prefill interference with concurrent decoding, without additional model calls or training. Across two models, two harnesses, and two benchmarks, Contexture improves throughput under SLO by 20-73% over the best of no eviction, harness compaction, AgentDiet, and Continuum, and by 7-63% over observation masking in five of eight configurations, and reduces GPU energy per completed session by up to 11%. It also raises throughput under SLO by 23% over LMCache alone on H100. Live-agent experiments show a mean accuracy improvement of 1.4 percentage points over unloaded no eviction, with a worst-case loss of 3.7 points, while observation masking loses 3-28 points.
item.dc:creator: Colin Hong, Bryan Shan, Wei Siong Pang, Chengzhi Lu, Xu Guo, Nitin Shivaraman, Tao Luo, Esha Choukse, Kisson Lin, Dmitrii Ustiugov

item.title: Exercised, Rarely Recovered: What Public Reports Say About Recovery in 50 AI Agent Harnesses and Runtimes
item.description: arXiv:2611.27090v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: When an AI coding agent deletes the wrong files or a long agent run crashes, users fall back on recovery mechanisms: resume from a checkpoint, undo, ask for approval, read the log. Research runtimes promise stronger guarantees, such as saga-style compensation and transactional rollback. We ask what public evidence shows about whether either kind works in real use. Under a protocol frozen before data collection, we graded 12 persistent agent runtimes, 26 coding-agent harnesses and 12 research runtimes on eight recovery mechanisms, from not found to exercised in a real run, with two blind coding passes, adjudication and re-verification against archived sources. Recovery is exercised almost everywhere in practice: 11 of 12 runtimes and 25 of 26 harnesses have at least one real-use report. Yet of 128 such reports, only 19 describe the run fully recovering; 54 are partial and 45 failed. Checkpoint/resume recovered once in 27 reports, rollback once in 15. Research runtimes show the opposite profile: guarantees evaluated on benchmarks, none reported in operation, and compensation of external effects, their central guarantee, is offered by no harness at all.
item.dc:creator: Kaviru Hapuarachchi

item.title: Omo: Giving Continuing AI-Agent Work a Place to Return To
item.description: arXiv:2611.27107v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: AI coding agents now keep working while the people who started them are away. Coming back is the hard part: a session list tells you which agent is where, but not what it was asked to do, what it changed, or what to tell it next. We present Omo, which gives each piece of continuing agent work a persistent place to return to. We built the idea twice. Omo Space is an open-source Minecraft mod in which rooms and screens that people build are live terminals on their own machine. Omo Theia brings the same rooms and desks into a customizable IDE, one step away from the editor and the Git patch. Both keep agent sessions running on the host after the view is closed. We describe the two systems, four lessons from building them, and a study designed to test whether returning to a place helps people pick up agent work correctly.
item.dc:creator: Kaviru Hapuarachchi, Harrison Edwards

item.title: OpenRing: Deadlock-Free Execution of Any Planner on AGV Floors with One-Way Lanes
item.description: arXiv:2611.27127v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Lifelong multi-agent path finding replans routes for automated guided vehicles, but deviations can invalidate a plan. With one-way lanes, a late vehicle or lost planner can close a ring of full segments. We separate how fast the floor runs from whether it keeps running. In OpenRing a planner proposes routes and an order, a local guard commits only moves and route changes that cannot close such a ring, and the order binds for a bounded time. Despite arbitrary proposals or planner loss, no ring closes. With two-place segments, traffic can continue under disturbances; progress is guaranteed once they end, and all vehicles exit if entries also stop. Among rules that reroute only on a proposal, every guard veto is necessary, and a clean plan keeps its crossing orders. The guarantee has a price: no rule that never stores a vehicle in a crossing under arbitrary stops carries more than $B/T_s$ per segment of $B$ places and traversal time $T_s$. With binding orders, three planners deadlock in 80 of 126 runs across eight floors. Inside OpenRing, none of the 126 runs deadlocks. OpenRing's closed-loop throughput rivals or exceeds the best baseline's. Physics simulations show no deadlocks or overlaps.
item.dc:creator: Zhihao Lin, Anh-Tu Nguyen, Hui Zhang, Yoshinobu Kawahara

item.title: Fix Where It Fails: Root-Cause-Guided Agentic Harness Optimization for Scene Graph Generation
item.description: arXiv:2611.27529v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Scene graph generation (SGG) aims to detect objects in an image and predict the relationships between them. The standard PredCls, SGCls, and SGDet settings show how much performance drops without ground-truth boxes and labels, but not where or why a model fails. Knowing this would allow fixing a model where it fails, without retraining. We propose RoHa-SGG (Root-cause-guided Harness optimization for SGG), which extends agentic harness optimization to SGG. It optimizes the harness, the inference code around a frozen SGG model. RoHa-SGG has two main LLM agents. A root-cause analysis (RCA) agent finds the components where the model fails and diagnoses why, and a proposer agent searches for a harness that fixes these causes. We evaluate RoHa-SGG on Visual Genome and PSG with representative two-stage, one-stage, and multimodal-LLM SGG models. The analysis shows that the components where ground-truth triplets are lost differ across models and datasets. RoHa-SGG improves every metric on all five model-dataset combinations. Graph-constrained R@100 and mR@100 rise by up to 15.8 and 26.4 points for the multimodal LLM and by up to 3.6 and 10.1 points for the two-stage and one-stage models. With root-cause guidance, the harness search reaches the final score of an unguided search up to three times faster.
item.dc:creator: Jee Eun Kim, Donghyeon Choi, Sangjune An, Hae Beom Lee, Kyong Hwan Jin

item.title: Joint Optimization of Fleet Size, Localization Infrastructure, and Trajectories for Multi-AUV Persistent Monitoring
item.description: arXiv:2611.27539v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Persistent monitoring of large-scale subsea infrastructure, such as offshore wind farm foundations, export cables, and inspection corridors, remains a fundamental challenge for autonomous underwater systems. The problem is not solely spatial coverage, but rather temporal coverage: ensuring that all relevant regions of interest are revisited within bounded time intervals under limited sensing, navigation uncertainty, and constrained vehicle resources. We compare three classes of trajectory strategies: (1) deterministic lane-based coverage (lawnmower patterns), (2) stochastic exploration (biased random walk with boundary constraints), and (3) coordinated partition-based strategies (Voronoi tessellation). Rather than seeking a universally superior method, we evaluate how varying levels of localization accuracy impact temporal coverage across two distinct operational profiles: persistent monitoring of the entire operational workspace versus targeted inspection of critical infrastructure. We present a simulation-based, quantitatively grounded study of temporal coverage in multi-AUV persistent monitoring, disentangling three interacting design dimensions: (i) trajectory generation strategy, (ii) fleet size, and (iii) localization accuracy provided by fixed acoustic beacon infrastructure. We introduce a cost-aware evaluation framework combining fleet size, number of beacons, and mission energy expenditure into a unified cost function. Results demonstrate that beyond a certain accuracy threshold, improvements in localization yield diminishing returns compared to coordinated trajectory design, an effect often obscured in integrated navigation-planning approaches. Coordinated-partition trajectories enable a reduced fleet size to achieve superior temporal coverage at a 39-46% lower overall life-cycle cost than rigid deterministic paths unoptimized for the localization infrastructure.
item.dc:creator: Jan Miko{\l}ajczyk, Jakub Ba{\l}enkowski, Maciej Borowiecki, Jan Ciecierski, Marcel Kolecki, Julian Maleta, Maksymilian Bernacki

item.title: Where Delay Compensation Belongs in a Decentralized Mean-Field-Game Swarm with a Control-Barrier Safety Filter
item.description: arXiv:2611.27540v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Large robot teams are often run as a plan-then-execute stack. We study a decentralized instance for drone swarms, a mean-field-game (MFG) routing field with a per-agent control-barrier-function (CBF) safety filter, when communication is limited by a shared TDMA channel. Neighbors are known only through noisy range and bearing measurements exchanged in round-robin slots, so the frame, and with it the age of every estimate, grows with swarm size. In simulation this delay reaches both layers but breaks only the safety layer. Without delay, swarms of up to 100 agents do not collide, even with each measurement's noise held for a whole frame; with it, stale estimates at the CBF cause collisions beyond a frame period of 125 to 175 ms, or 75 to 100 ms at 100 agents with held noise, and swarm size sets where that limit lies and how steeply collisions rise. At the MFG, staleness makes the local density noisier without biasing it, and throughput drops by at most a tenth. We then compensate with lightweight on-board predictors, from constant-velocity fits to a small learned network, that estimate each neighbor's position from its last broadcasts. A layer-split experiment shows where prediction is needed: at the CBF it restores safety and extends the tolerated frame period by 1.4 to 1.7 times with an untrained constant-velocity fit and about 2.3 with the learned network when the noise is redrawn each step; with noise held for a frame the two extend it about equally, while at the MFG it only refines the congestion correction. A constant wider safety margin, the simplest alternative, makes collisions more frequent in a bottleneck. With the routing solved offline, that layer is robust to the delay because it sees neighbors only through a crowd average; compensation belongs in the safety filter, switched on only above the uncompensated limit, since below it the predictor's own error adds collisions.
item.dc:creator: Jan Miko{\l}ajczyk, Igor Rostkowski, Bartosz Og\'orkiewicz, Szymon Skierski, Sylwia Opat, Wojciech Rybak, Miko{\l}aj Sczogiel, Rados{\l}aw Pa{\l}ys, Jan Gogulski, Bartosz Ko\'scio{\l}ek, Andrzej Pijanowski, Szymon Kowalski, Marcin Misiewicz

item.title: Embodied-Harness: Towards Recursive Self-Improvement for Robotic Manipulation
item.description: arXiv:2611.27689v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Vision-language model (VLM)-based agents offer a promising approach to robotic manipulation, yet remain limited by inadequate memory organization, uncertain failure attribution, and limited reuse of execution experience. We propose Embodied-Harness, a dual-agent framework that improves manipulation by refining the execution harness without updating model parameters. The Actor interacts with the environment through a robot-control interface, while the Reflector converts execution evidence into reusable operational guidance. Hierarchical Memory Architecture maintains short-term execution context and long-term experiential knowledge to support execution and reflection. Evidence-based Experience Reflection grounds failure diagnosis in observed interactions, while Recursive Harness Self-Improvement refines operational guidance across successive attempts. Experiments on RoboTwin 2.0, RoboSPA, and RMBench demonstrate the effectiveness of Embodied-Harness in generalization under environmental variations, spatial reasoning, long-horizon planning, and memory-dependent manipulation. Our method achieves success rates of 82.4%, 76.7%, and 94.4% on the three benchmarks, respectively. Real-world evaluation further yields an average success rate of 96.7% across three manipulation tasks. These results highlight the potential of Embodied-Harness to improve robotic manipulation through experience-driven harness self-improvement.
item.dc:creator: Zhenxuan Fan, Zhuoya Wang, Yuqian Yuan, Wenqiao Zhang, Juncheng Li, Jun Xiao, Siliang Tang, Yueting Zhuang

item.title: Beyond Self-Critique: Epistemic Convergence Control for Multi-Agent Research Verification
item.description: arXiv:2611.27839v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Multi-agent systems for scientific claim verification increasingly rely on role-structured LLM debate to pressure-test hypotheses. However, when debating agents are instantiated from the same underlying base model, they share identical latent representations, making self-critique bias structurally inevitable. Static fixed-iteration protocols compound this by either halting prematurely before evidence stabilizes or wasting inference compute after convergence. We present \sys{}, a multi-agent research verification framework that addresses both failure modes. First, we introduce an asymmetric role architecture comprising an Advocate, Skeptic, and Arbitrator with opposing epistemic directives, producing significantly lower role-embedding similarity (0.852 vs.\ 0.918 for symmetric Multi-Agent Debate [MAD], $p = 5.82 \times 10^{-8}$) and surfacing more contested claims (22.0\% vs.\ 15.4\%). Second, we propose the Belief-Delta ($\DB$) convergence criterion, an evidence-grounded stopping rule that eliminates over-iteration (0.0\% vs.\ 62.5\% for Fixed-$3$) while cutting LLM calls by 2.4$\times$. Third, each supported claim is anchored to a verbatim literature snippet audited by an independent NLI classifier, achieving a 21.7\% hallucination rate (comparable to 25.9\% for a Self-Refine critic, $p = 0.61$) while establishing auditable evidence grounding. Across 200 runs on 40 research hypotheses evaluated with DeepSeek-R1-32B, \sys{} balances compute efficiency with rigorous epistemic verification.
item.dc:creator: Chrisantus Eze

item.title: LesionAgent: Training-Free Agentic Tumor Tracking and Response Assessment in Longitudinal CT
item.description: arXiv:2611.27876v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Every few months, a cancer patient's CT scans decide whether treatment continues. 3D foundation models can now detect, segment, register and track lesions, yet none of them reads the scans as a radiologist does. A radiologist decides which findings are lesions, which are the same lesion months later and whether a new spot means progression, and checks each decision against the extensive rules of a clinical guideline. We introduce LesionAgent, an LLM agent that performs this read end to end without task-specific training. It operates frozen 3D models as tools, acts in 3D through coordinate-labelled views, remembers every lesion across visits in a registry, verifies every model output it relies on, and leaves every number to a deterministic guideline engine. On four public longitudinal CT datasets, LesionAgent tracks more lesions and measures them more accurately than every automatic baseline, and where the same 3D models chained by fixed rules call progression falsely at 33 of 56 follow-ups, it does so twice. On clinical follow-up CTs, it agrees with the radiologists' response at 20 of 23 follow-ups, including every change in response, and without training on DeepLesion, it retrieves more of its lesions than every tracker trained on it (89.0% vs. 87.4%). Its harness, not its LLM, makes the difference: given the same LLM and 3D models but not the harness, Claude Code reaches a detection F1 of 41% and LesionAgent 78%, and an open-weight LLM that can run inside the hospital rises from 6% to 73%. LesionAgent and a napari reading app for any LLM are available at https://github.com/MIC-DKFZ/LesionAgent.
item.dc:creator: Maximilian Rokuss, Jeya Maria Jose Valanarasu, Alejandro Lozano, Benjamin Hamm, Yannick Kirchhoff, Fabian Isensee, Klaus Maier-Hein

item.title: MetaShare: Failure-Aware Collective Self-Improvement for Open-Ended Agents
item.description: arXiv:2610.21887v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Humans often learn fastest not by repeating success, but by remembering which failures not to repeat. Open-ended self-improving agents can share experience across lineages, as in GEA, or edit their own improvement mechanisms, as in DGM-Hyperagents, yet failed improvement attempts are rarely retained as reusable cross-branch knowledge, and search can collapse onto redundant strategies. We introduce MetaShare, a failure-aware framework that records successful and unsuccessful agent modifications together with signed performance deltas. Before each generation, MetaShare retrieves diverse high-performing strategies alongside high-confidence failures from other lineages, letting agents reuse effective mechanisms while avoiding known dead ends. A task-blind auditor periodically injects absent or underrepresented mechanism categories, while embedding-based de-ranking limits redundancy during retrieval. Multiple meta-agents propose modifications in parallel at heterogeneous temperatures behind a deterministic selector that gates applicability, scope, compilability, and size. Experiments across paper review, coding, math grading, robotics reward design, and financial audit-risk assessment show that MetaShare's median matches or exceeds DGM-Hyperagents' final performance and reaches its own best-performing agent in 1.7--2.9$\times$ fewer evolution iterations.
item.dc:creator: Vishal Bhutani, Prasang Gupta, Sumanth Chundru, Kevin Paul

item.title: Trilemma: How Agents choose between Honesty, Confidentiality, and Task Completion
item.description: arXiv:2611.08312v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Personal AI agents often act on underspecified instructions and use context such as previous conversations to decide how to proceed. This context may contain private preferences that influence the assigned task or the relation to other people. When asked by a third party to justify its choices, the agent might be conflicted between honesty, confidentiality and task completion. Prior work has studied these largely as separate problems. We study deception and leakage of private information together in a simulated company Slack workspace. There, four employees delegate a sprint staffing to their personal agents. From private messages, two of these agents learn that their employee avoids working with a particular colleague. Since the agents are asked to justify their task preferences and the true justification is confidential, the agent cannot simultaneously be honest, preserve confidentiality, and complete the staffing. We evaluate 9 open-weight and closed models. Of the 135 (out of 140) open-weight agents that pursue the avoidance preference, 107 either make false claims about task fit or logistics or cite a true consideration as if it were their actual reason. Confidentiality instructions reduce disclosure of the preference from 71% (none) to 29% (medium) to 1% (strong). However, the sprint staffing is often not completed anyway, since neither agent concedes. In their reasoning, agents engage in motivated reasoning by frequently acknowledging evidence against their claims and still concluding that the claims are not false. Our results indicate that agents can make false or misleading claims in a day-to-day task without being instructed to. This environment provides a testbed for deception monitors and studying how agents resolve value conflicts.
item.dc:creator: Johannes Taraz, Abhinav Kumar, Sahar Abdelnabi

item.title: Binary Decision Process in Pre-Evacuation Behavior
item.description: arXiv:2508.08284v5 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: In crowd evacuation the time interval before decisive movement towards a safe place is defined as the pre-evacuation phase, and it has crucial impact on the total time required for safe egress. This process mainly refers to situation awareness and response to an external stressors, e.g., fire alarms. Due to the complexity of human cognitive process, simulation is used to study this important time interval. In this paper a binary decision process is formulated to simulate pre-evacuation time of many evacuees in a given social context. The model combines the classic opinion dynamics (the French-DeGroot model) with binary phase transition to describe how group pre-evacuation time emerges from individual interaction. The model parameters are quantitatively meaningful to human factors research within socio-psychological background, e.g., whether an individual is stubborn or open-minded, or what kind of the social topology exists among the individuals and how it matters in aggregating individuals into social groups. The modeling framework also describes collective motion of many evacuee agents in a planar space, and the resulting multi-agent system is partly similar to the Vicsek flocking model, and it is meaningful to explore complex social behavior during phase transition of a non-equilibrium process.
item.dc:creator: Peng N. Wang, Peter B. Luh, Peter Sincak, Laura Pitukova, Xuesong Lu, W. M. Wonham, Timo Korhonen

item.title: AgentArk: Distilling Multi-Agent Intelligence into a Single LLM Agent
item.description: arXiv:2602.03955v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: While large language model (LLM) multi-agent systems achieve superior reasoning performance through iterative debate, practical deployment is limited by their high computational cost and error propagation. This paper proposes AgentArk, a novel framework to distill multi-agent dynamics into the weights of a single model, effectively transforming explicit test-time interactions into implicit model capabilities. This equips a single agent with the intelligence of multi-agent systems while remaining computationally efficient. Specifically, we investigate three hierarchical distillation strategies across various models, tasks, scaling, and scenarios: reasoning-enhanced fine-tuning; trajectory-based augmentation; and process-aware distillation. By shifting the burden of computation from inference to training, the distilled models preserve the efficiency of one agent while exhibiting strong reasoning and self-correction performance of multiple agents. They further demonstrate enhanced robustness and generalization across diverse reasoning tasks. We hope this work can shed light on future research on efficient and robust multi-agent development. Our code is at https://github.com/AIFrontierLab/AgentArk.
item.dc:creator: Yinyi Luo, Yiqiao Jin, Weichen Yu, Mengqi Zhang, Srijan Kumar, Xiaoxiao Li, Weijie Xu, Xin Chen, Jindong Wang

item.title: GAAMA: Graph Augmented Associative Memory for Agents
item.description: arXiv:2603.27910v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: AI agents that talk with users across many sessions need long-term memory to stay coherent and personalized. Existing approaches use either flat retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) that ignores how memories connect, or entity-centric knowledge graphs. Entity-centric graphs split each message into separate triples, which loses its context, and in conversations the speakers become hubs linked to almost every message, so propagation through them tells retrieval little. We present GAAMA, a graph-augmented associative memory that organizes conversations around topics. It keeps verbatim episodes, uses an LLM to distill them into atomic facts and topic concepts, and then synthesizes higher-order reflections. These four node types are linked by five kinds of structural edges, and topic concepts supply the cross-cutting paths, so mega-hubs do not form. Retrieval blends nearest-neighbor similarity search with Personalized PageRank whose transitions depend on edge type. We also introduce GRAFT (Graph Repair by Augmenting Facts & Topology), an offline repair step: for questions whose retrieved evidence fell short, a bounded ReAct agent searches memory again and records the grounded answer as a fresh fact, so later questions find it directly without extra query-time cost. On LoCoMo10, GAAMA achieves the highest average score of all compared methods (79.1%) and is competitive in every question category; GRAFT adds a small further gain. In a controlled comparison, replacing GAAMA's concept-linked facts with entity relation triples lowers reward by 3.0 pp. On MemoryArena, scored on what memory alone determines, GAAMA has the best score on average.
item.dc:creator: Swarna Kamal Paul, Shubhendu Sharma, Nitin Sareen

item.title: GENSTRAT: Toward a Science of Strategic Reasoning in Large Language Models
item.description: arXiv:2605.23238v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Fixed game suites for evaluating strategic reasoning in large language models (LLMs) saturate and are hard to keep free of contamination. We introduce GENSTRAT, a system for evaluating the strategic capabilities of LLMs driven by procedural generation of two-player zero-sum imperfect-information betting games, allowing an evaluator to draw novel, fresh games on demand. Each game is characterized on a scale of five complexity axes (state space, temporal contingency, opponent dependence, private information, precision) and measured by Monte Carlo simulation. Using this generator, we construct a 50-game benchmark and hold a tournament of twelve frontier and open-weight models, gathering data from over 40,000 LLM vs. LLM matches. We further construct a composite complexity axis, and find that, on the eight hardest games, the gap between the best and worst model is 1.7x its value across the whole set of games (1.6x with held-out weights or with hard games chosen by the outcome-free temporal axis alone, and 1.35x with payoffs scaled by their random-play standard deviation). Ablations show that a higher thinking budget, disclosing the opponent's strategy, and higher reasoning matched to a game's specific demands (for private information and planning depth) were associated with higher margins for the LLM player. On 27 solved games, frontier models play at the value of the equilibrium while weaker models lose to it, and the leaderboard predicts strength on fresh games and on six new games, even after controlling for a general-capability leaderboard.
item.dc:creator: Vartan Shadarevian, Kia Ghods, Alex Kenich, Anany Kotawala

item.title: SYSEVOLVE: Safe, Autonomous Attack-Defense Co-evolution for Evolving Cyber Defense
item.description: arXiv:2608.15012v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The offensive capability of large language models (LLMs) has crossed from research demonstration into documented reality. Frontier models have autonomously breached real production systems, and open-weight models now deliver frontier-level exploitation at negligible cost. Existing defenses cannot keep pace with such attacks: human-intensive defense updates over days to weeks, while AI-based defense, on the other side, trained on fixed historical data, does not adapt to an evolving attacker. We trace these persistent failures to one root cause: defense evolves in isolation, cut off from the adversary that should be driving its evolution. That isolation manifests at three layers: the deployment layer, the capability layer, and the adversarial layer. To build a defense that evolves at the speed of attack, we propose co-evolution as the integrating insight, replacing isolated evolution with mutual driving between attack and defense. Based on this insight, we present SysEvolve, a safe and autonomous co-evolutionary system built from three co-designed components, SysField, SysSpear, and SysArmor. SysField constructs realistic multi-host ranges via declarative topology-driven construction. SysSpear generates efficient, safe attack schemes via task-sliced local search, a bidirectional expert-knowledge base, and static-analysis verification. SysArmor performs real-time, interpretable defense via state tracking, CTI-context fusion, and stage-matched response. In evaluation, SysField achieves zero-loss collection at 2.1\% overhead and orchestrates 257 CVEs into 1,148 ranges. SysSpear improves red-team success by over 25\%, attains the best completion on complex multi-vulnerability ranges. SysArmor achieves 10--1000$\times$ greater precision than prior systems and detects real APT attacks in production at Huawei and Sangfor. Our evaluation also reveals four findings about LLM agent capabilities.
item.dc:creator: Yuhan Meng, Jiandong Jin, Shaofei Li, Jionghao Huang, Puyi Wang, Hanlin Jiang, Anis Yusof, Peng Jiang, Changling Zhou, Zhenkai Liang, Yao Guo, Ding Li

item.title: Codetta: High-Capacity, Keyless, and Undetectable Multi-Agent Collusion
item.description: arXiv:2609.28900v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Multi-agent systems built on large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in high-stakes settings such as finance, healthcare, and software engineering, where agents coordinate through natural-language messages. The same channels, however, let colluding agents exfiltrate confidential information or coordinate unauthorized actions, and steganography can hide such communication inside outputs that look ordinary to an auditor reading the transcript. Existing provably undetectable LLM steganography protocols are not suited to realistic deployments. High-capacity schemes assume a symmetric setting where the receiver can reproduce the sender's output distribution, the state-of-the-art protocol for asymmetric agents has very low capacity, and most approaches rely on a pre-shared secret key. We make the threat of undetectable agent collusion concrete with Codetta, a high-capacity steganographic protocol for independently deployed agents in realistic asymmetric settings. Codetta combines a shared public model that estimates the communication channel, a sampling mechanism that preserves the sender's output distribution, and an adaptive error-correcting code. It further removes the pre-shared key through a steganographic key exchange that lets independently deployed agents establish a shared key while keeping the transcript computationally indistinguishable from ordinary model outputs. Across three agent workloads and three sender models, Codetta achieves up to $102\times$ the capacity of the state-of-the-art asymmetric protocol, and its key exchange establishes a shared key with about 80k visible tokens at an empirically certified failure probability of at most $4.1\times 10^{-3}$. These results show that effectively undetectable collusion is becoming feasible between independently deployed agents, so auditing must go beyond inspecting communication transcripts.
item.dc:creator: Qi Pang, Virginia Smith, Wenting Zheng
